q: 1. The bond in which each course consists of alternate stretchers and headers is known as ..........
explain: In Flemish bond, headers and stretchers alternate within every single course, giving it a more decorative appearance than English bond.

q: 2. The bond in which the bonding bricks are at an inclination to the direction of the wall is known as...
explain: Raking bonds (like herring-bone or diagonal bond) place bricks at an angle to the wall's face to improve longitudinal strength.

q: 3. The English bond in which the corners of the wall are strengthened by starting every stretcher course with a three fourth bat at the quoin and a header is placed next to the three fourth bat at the quoin in alternate stretcher course is called ..........
explain: Dutch bond is a variation of English bond that uses a specific arrangement of bats and headers at the quoin to improve appearance and strength.

q: 4. The English bond in which queen closers are placed next to quoin headers and a header is introduced next to the quoin stretcher in every alternate stretcher course ..........
explain: English cross bond is similar to English bond but staggers the stretcher courses by introducing an extra header at the quoin, creating a distinctive pattern.

q: 5. A bond in which a header course is provided only after few stretcher courses is known as ..........
explain: Garden wall bond is used for thin walls; it usually consists of one course of headers for every three or five courses of stretchers.

q: 6. A brick masonry could fail due to ..........
options: rupture along a vertical joint in poorly bonded walls
explain: Brick walls can fail through crushing under heavy loads, sliding (shearing) between bricks, or splitting along vertical joints (rupture).

q: 7. Good bonding in the brick masonry is ensured when ..........
options: all bricks used are of uniform size
the vertical joints in alternate courses are in plumb from top to base
bats are used as sparingly as possible
explain: Strength in masonry comes from uniform materials, vertical alignment of joints (plumb), and minimizing the use of broken bricks (bats).

q: 8. Which of the following is not a tool used in laying brick wall
explain: An auger is a drilling tool used for soil or wood; it is not used in bricklaying like a trowel or plumb bob.

q: 9. A bonding in which all courses are laid as stretchers is known as ..........
explain: Stretcher bond (or running bond) is composed entirely of stretchers and is only used for thin walls.

q: 10. A bond in which stretcher bricks are laid on edge in alternate courses forming continuous cavity is known as ..........
explain: Soldier bond involves bricks laid vertically on their ends (on edge), often used for decorative purposes or window sills.

q: 11. A temporary structure erected with a purpose of providing a safe working platform is known as .......
explain: Scaffolding is the temporary framework used by workers to reach high sections of a building during construction or repair.

q: 12. An arrangement for supporting an unsafe structure temporarily, till it is rendered safe or dismantled, is known as ..........
explain: Shoring is the use of temporary supports (shores) to stabilize a building that is in danger of collapsing or undergoing renovation.

q: 13. The compressive strength of first class and second class bricks should not be less than ..........
explain: Indian Standards typically specify that first-class bricks should have a minimum compressive strength of 105 kg/cm², but commonly 80-100 kg/cm² is cited as the safe minimum for structural work.

q: 14. When two walls separated by a small gap, are connected together by metal pins, it is called .......
explain: A cavity wall consists of two leaves of masonry separated by an air space (cavity) and connected by metal wall ties.

q: 15. Minimum width of load bearing wall should be
explain: A standard load-bearing brick wall is usually at least one full brick thick (roughly 230mm including plaster).

q: 16. Cavity walls ..........
options: prevent dampness from entering the building
have lesser dead load for given wall thickness
are better insulated against heat and sound
explain: The air gap in cavity walls prevents moisture transfer (dampness) and acts as an insulator for heat and noise.

q: 17. A wall which is constructed to divide the space within the building into rooms is called ..........
explain: Partition walls are non-load-bearing internal walls used to create separate rooms within a structure.

q: 18. A load bearing partition wall is called ..........
explain: While many partitions are non-load-bearing, if an internal wall carries structural weight, it is referred to as an internal load-bearing wall.

q: 19. Brick masonry constructed within a framework of wooden member to act as a partition wall is called ..........
explain: Brick nogging is a type of wall construction where bricks are used to fill the spaces between timber studs in a wood frame.

q: 20. The member laid horizontally to support common rafters and which transmits the loads to the trusses or wall are
explain: Purlins are horizontal beams that run parallel to the ridge to support the common rafters.

q: 21. The minimum thickness of a wall in stone masonry cannot be less than
explain: Because stone units are large and irregular, stone masonry walls must have a minimum thickness (usually 35-40 cm) to ensure stability.

q: 22. The upper horizontal portion of the step where the foot is placed while ascending or descending is known as ..........
explain: The tread is the flat horizontal surface of a stair step that you walk on.

q: 23. Brick lintels are used when the span is ..........
explain: Brick lintels are weak in tension and are only suitable for small openings, typically less than 1 meter.

q: 24. The highest point of an arch is called
explain: The crown is the highest point of the arch, where the keystone is typically located.

q: 25. The inner curve of an arch is known as ..........
explain: The intrados is the lower or inner curve of an arch. The underside surface itself is often called the soffit.

q: 26. The wedge shaped units of masonry forming an arch are called ..........
explain: Voussoirs are the individual wedge-shaped blocks (stones or bricks) that make up the body of an arch.

q: 27. Spandril is ..........
options: the curved space formed between the extrados and the horizontal line through the crown
the space in the form of a sector between the intrados and the center of the arch
the curved space between the intrados and springing line
explain: A spandril is the triangular-like space between the outer curve (extrados) of an arch and a rectangular enclosure or horizontal line.

q: 28. A temporary rigid structure having platform to enable masons to work at different stages of a building is known as
explain: Scaffolding is the temporary framework used to support workers and materials during the construction or repair of a building.

q: 29. A row of arches in continuation is called ..........
explain: An arcade is a succession of arches, each spanning an opening and supported by columns or piers.

q: 30. A junction at which two walls meet at an angle other than 90° is called
explain: A squint junction occurs when walls meet at an acute or obtuse angle, requiring special 'squint' bricks.

q: 31. The points from which the curve of arch springs at the supports are called ..........
explain: Springing points are the specific points where the arch begins to curve away from the support.

q: 32. The inclined surface on the abutment which acts as a seat for the arch is known as ..........
explain: The skewback is the sloped surface on the abutment from which the arch units start their curve.

q: 33. For a building one side of the busy street where the ordinary scaffolding will obstruct the traffic on the road, the type of scaffolding provided is
explain: Needle scaffolding (cantilever scaffolding) is supported by 'needles' passing through the wall, keeping the ground level clear for traffic.

q: 34. The rise of the arch is defined as the clear vertical distance between ..........
options: the springing line and the highest point on extrados
the springing line and the highest point on intrados
the center of the arch and the crown of the arch
explain: Rise is measured vertically from the horizontal line connecting the springing points (springing line) to the highest point of the intrados.

q: 35. A brick which is cut in such a way that the width of its one end is half that is a full brick is called
explain: A king closer is created by cutting off a triangular corner so that one header end and one stretcher end are half-width.

q: 36. An arch which is formed by two arcs of circles meeting at the apex point is known as ..........
explain: Pointed arches consist of two intersecting curves, typical in Gothic architecture.

q: 37. In a pointed arch if the apex point and the springing points become corners of an isosceles triangle, then it is known as ..........
explain: A lancet arch is a narrow, tall pointed arch where the height is much greater than the width.

q: 38. The pointed arch in which the depth is more at the crown than at the springing is known as ..........
explain: In a variable depth arch, the thickness of the arch rings changes throughout its span, usually being thicker at the crown.

q: 39. The bearing of the lintel should be
explain: The minimum bearing (overlap on the wall) for a lintel is usually 10 cm, the height of the lintel, or 1/12th of the span—whichever is greatest.

q: 40. If the center of the arch lies on the springing line, it is ..........
explain: A semi-circular arch has its center exactly on the line connecting the two springing points.

q: 41. If the center of the arch lies above the springing line, it is ..........
explain: In a horse-shoe arch, the curve continues past the semi-circle, meaning the center is above the line where it starts curving inward.

q: 42. If the center of the arch lies below the springing line, it is ..........
explain: A segmental arch is less than a semi-circle, meaning its center point is located below the springing line.

q: 43. An arch in the form of a perfect circle used for circular windows is called ..........
explain: A bull's eye arch is a complete 360-degree circular arch often used for aesthetic ventilation or windows.

q: 44. An arch which is constructed either on a flat arch or on a wooden lintel to provide greater strength is called ..........
explain: A relieving arch is built above a lintel or flat arch to divert the weight of the wall above to the side supports.

q: 45. The angle of the skew-back with the horizontal in the case of flat arches is usually ..........
explain: For flat arches, the skewback is typically cut at a 60-degree angle to the horizontal to create a stable base for the compression units.

q: 46. The portion of the wall which supports an arch is termed as ..........
explain: The abutment is the end support of an arch that resists both the vertical load and the horizontal thrust.

q: 47. The vertical distance between the tops of two successive treads is called ..........
explain: Rise is the vertical height of a single step in a staircase.

q: 48. Normally the rise of the steps would be between ..........
explain: A rise of 10-15 cm is standard for public buildings, while 15-18 cm is common for residential; 10-15 cm is generally safer and more comfortable.

q: 49. The live load on the floors of residential buildings, hospital wards, private sitting room in hostels should be
explain: The standard design live load for residential areas and private rooms is 2.0 kN/m² (approx 200 Kg/m²).

q: 50. When the two blocks of stone have a tendency to be pulled apart in the direction of their lengths, then the type of joint to be used should be
explain: A cramped joint uses a metal 'cramp' to tie two stones together, preventing them from being pulled apart by tension.
